report.verdict: October 2026 was the District's largest month on record by handle ($95.76m) but growth has stalled at +0.9% YoY, hold is flat at 8.8%, and tax take fell 1.7% as volume shifted toward the 20%-taxed venue books. The bigger story is regulatory: B26-0656 (online casino at 25% GGR plus 4% of assessments, sweepstakes folded into licensing, gambling age to 21) cleared committee 3-1 on 18 Nov and must survive two full-Council readings before the Council period closes in mid-December. For a would-be entrant, DC is a ~$90m-GGR, seven-brand, FanDuel-dominated market where the 30% Class C tax and $2m licence make a mobile-only sportsbook entry marginal; the credible angles are B2B supply or an iGaming licence if the bill lands.

summary: **Record handle, no growth:** OLG's unaudited October 2026 report shows District-wide sports wagering handle of $95.76m across 2.95m wagers, the highest month since launch but only +0.9% YoY (Oct-25: $94.89m) and +19.3% MoM on the NFL/NBA calendar. GGR was $8.46m (+1.1% YoY, +51.8% MoM) at an 8.83% hold (Oct-25: 8.81%; Sep-26: 6.94%). Tax collected was $1.94m, −1.7% YoY, because growth came from Class A venue books taxed at 20% rather than Class C mobile-only books taxed at 30%.

**CY2026 on course for a record on handle, not on GGR:** January–October handle is $724.05m (+3.8% YoY) but GGR is $70.16m at a 9.69% hold versus 11.1% for CY2025 (handle $855.6m, GGR $94.4m, tax $22.06m). The District needs $131.6m in Nov–Dec to beat 2025's handle (Nov–Dec 2025 delivered $158.3m); on our estimate CY2026 ends at ~$885–890m handle but only ~$86–88m GGR and ~$21m tax, both below 2025 (estimate).

**FY2026 (Oct-25 to Sep-26) closed strongly:** summing OLG's per-operator fiscal-year totals gives handle $881.45m (+9.9% vs FY2025's $801.9m), GGR $91.50m (10.4% hold) and tax $21.97m (+13.3% vs $19.39m), a blended 24.0% effective rate on GGR. October is month one of FY2027.

**A mobile market with a venue-licensing skin:** OLG's FY2025 report puts online handle at $773.2m (96.4%) versus $28.7m retail (3.6%); online generated 96% of sports-wagering tax. Monthly OLG reports do not split Class A operators' retail and mobile volumes, so the retail share is a fiscal-year figure only.

**Regulator and law:** the Office of Lottery and Gaming (OLG), an agency under the DC Office of the Chief Financial Officer, is both lottery operator and sports-wagering regulator. The framework is the Sports Wagering Lottery Amendment Act of 2018 (DC Code § 36-621.01 et seq.) and 30 DCMR Chapter 21, overhauled by the Sports Wagering Amendment Act of 2024 (effective 15 Jul 2024), which replaced the District-operated GambetDC monopoly with private District-wide mobile licences.

**Three licence classes, all five-year terms (DC Code § 36-621.06; OLG Licensing page):** Class A for designated venues (Capital One Arena, Audi Field, Nationals Park, St. Elizabeths East arena) at $1.0m initial / $0.5m renewal with District-wide mobile rights; Class B for retail-only venues outside a two-block radius of a Class A facility at $100k / $50k; Class C for team-linked mobile-only operators at $2.0m / $1.0m. CBE-majority joint ventures pay $250k (A) or $25k (B). Licences are non-transferable; provisional licences run six months.

**Tax is on GGR, graded by class, no loss carry-forward observed:** Class A 20%, Class B 10%, Class C 30% of gross sports wagering revenue, filed monthly on form FR-426G by the 20th. Fanatics booked negative GGR (−$48k) in September and paid tax of exactly 30.0% of its positive October GGR, i.e. no offset of prior-month losses. The blended rate was 22.9% in October and 24.0% CY-to-date.

**Seven live brands, two of them are the market:** FanDuel (Audi Field, Class A) took 44.8% of October handle ($42.95m) and 59.5% of GGR ($5.03m) on an 11.72% hold; DraftKings (Class C) 27.7% / 19.7% on 6.26%; Caesars (Capital One Arena) 10.3% / 4.7% on 4.04%; Fanatics 9.3% / 7.2%; BetMGM (Nationals Park) 6.2% / 6.8%; bet365 1.7% / 2.2% in its first full month; Sports & Social (U Street, Class B) $21.5k handle. Top-two share: 72.6% of handle, 79.2% of GGR. FanDuel alone paid 52% of October tax.

**Churn at the margin:** PENN's theScore Bet (ex-ESPN Bet, launched Jan 2025) ceased DC operations on 23 Feb 2026 after 13 months; bet365 (Hillside LLC) launched 8 Sep 2026 with a Monumental Sports & Entertainment partnership (Capitals, Wizards, Mystics) and reached $1.59m handle at 11.56% hold in October. Four Class B venues listed in September (Grand Central, Cloakbook, Grand Central H Street, Ugly Mug) reported zero activity and were dropped from the October report.

**Sharp-money tell in the venue books:** Caesars' October bet count fell 75.7% YoY while handle rose 21% to $9.82m, pushing average stake to $103 and hold to 4.0% (11.1% a year ago; GGR −56%). DraftKings' bet count fell 55% while average stake doubled to $37.45 and hold compressed to 6.3%. FanDuel's 11.7% hold on a $23.77 average stake is the recreational benchmark the others are not matching.

**Lottery is the other half of OLG's book and it is shrinking:** FY2025 lottery operating revenue was $210.7m, net revenue $83.4m, and the General Fund transfer $32.5m — down 17.4% from $39.35m in FY2024 per the DC OIG-commissioned audit. Adding $19.3m of sports-wagering tax, total regulated-gaming transfers were $51.8m, the highest since FY2017. Cumulative lottery contributions since 1982: $2.43bn.

**iGaming is one vote series from the finish line:** B26-0656, the Internet Gaming and Consumer Protection Act of 2026 (CM Wendell Felder, introduced 9 Apr 2026, hearing 4 May), passed the Committee on Human Services 3-1 on 18 Nov 2026 (CM Henderson against). Committee print: 25% tax on adjusted gross internet gaming revenue, 12.5% on live-dealer, plus 2% community-impact and 2% regulatory assessments; $2m application fee and $1m five-year renewal; maximum two brands per licensee; in-District live-dealer studio with a labor-peace agreement; supplier licence $50k / $25k. It needs two full-Council readings before the Council period ends in mid-December, then Mayoral signature and the 30-day Congressional review.

**The committee rewrote two things that matter:** sweepstakes/dual-currency casinos would be licensed and taxed as iGaming rather than banned outright, and the minimum age for all non-lottery gambling (including sports betting) would rise from 18 to 21. The CFO's fiscal note scores the bill at +$62.6m net revenue over FY2027–30 ($47.3m gaming tax), net of a $3.4m lottery-earnings loss and $1.8m of lost sports-wagering tax from the age change.

**Prediction markets are an untaxed overhang:** as of 25 Nov 2026 all Kalshi and Polymarket markets, including sports event contracts, are live in DC — the CFTC's home jurisdiction — with no District enforcement action identified, in contrast to Washington State's court-ordered halt. DFS also operates without a DC-specific geofence. Neither pays the 20–30% GGR tax.

**Payments are card/ACH-based and permissive:** DC imposes no credit-card funding ban (CASPR scorecard), no deposit-to-bet waiting period and no in-play restrictions; operators must verify identity and location, with new customers allowed to deposit and wager for 30 days before completing verification (or before first withdrawal). Statutory minimum age is 18; BetMGM and Caesars self-impose 21.

**Responsible gambling and advertising are rule-based but light:** 30 DCMR §§ 2128–2131 require an OLG-approved responsible-gaming plan, helpline information on all advertising, balanced win/lose messaging and an OLG-licensed statement; Class B operators may not place physical advertising within two blocks of a Class A venue; a single District-wide self-exclusion list covers lottery, iLottery, retail and mobile sports betting with terms from 18 months to lifetime (secondary source). CASPR grades DC 'F' on consumer-protection breadth.

**Political direction is expansion with a higher consumer-protection floor, not tax hikes:** the Council moved from a protectionist lottery monopoly (2019–24) to an open, high-tax private model (2024), and is now pushing iGaming plus sweepstakes regulation plus age 21. No pending change to sports-wagering tax rates or fees was found. OLG's Executive Director (Thomas 'Randy' Burnside) has backed iGaming despite acknowledged iLottery cannibalisation.

**Read-through for B2Tech:** at October run-rates a 5% handle share equals ~$57m annual handle, ~$5.5m GGR at the market's 9.7% YTD hold and ~$3.9m after 30% Class C tax — before marketing, the $2m licence and a mandatory team tie-up (estimate). A direct mobile sportsbook entry does not clear a sensible hurdle rate. The actionable options are (i) B2B platform/managed-services to a Class A/B venue or a Class C team partner, (ii) an iGaming operator or $50k supplier licence if B26-0656 passes (two brands per licence, preference language for existing sports licensees in the bill as introduced), and (iii) using DC as a low-cost regulatory reference licence rather than a P&L market.

segments.name: Sports betting — market structure, operators and the October 2026 result
segments.headline: A record $95.8m month that masks flat growth, a 9.7% YTD hold and a two-operator market in which FanDuel's venue licence delivers 60% of GGR at a 20% tax rate.
narrative: OLG's unaudited October 2026 filing (posted 20 Nov 2026) records 2,952,180 wagers, handle of $95,757,609, payouts of $87,300,236, GGR of $8,457,374 and tax of $1,936,511 across seven reporting licensees. Against October 2025 (handle $94.89m, GGR $8.36m, tax $1.97m per the OLG series as compiled by Sports Handle and Covers, which differ from each other by under $1k) that is +0.9% on handle, +1.1% on GGR and −1.7% on tax. Against October 2024 (handle $65.8m) the two-year growth is +45.5%, so the market has plateaued after the 2024–25 step-change that followed the opening of District-wide mobile to private operators. Month-on-month the jump is seasonal: September handle was $80.24m at a 6.94% hold; October added NBA and NHL tip-off to a full NFL slate and the hold normalised to 8.83%.

FanDuel, operating under the Audi Field Class A licence, is the market. Its October handle fell 4.9% YoY to $42.95m but a hold of 11.72% (Oct-25: 8.8%) lifted GGR 26% to $5.03m, giving it 44.8% of handle and 59.5% of GGR; its $1.01m of tax was 52% of the District's take despite the lower 20% rate. Year-to-date FanDuel holds 41.8% of handle and 55.5% of GGR on a 12.84% hold, with 12.85m wagers at an average stake of $23.58. This is a recreational, parlay-heavy book: the average stake is the lowest of any operator and the hold is the highest. Its position is structural, not cyclical: it inherited the OLG customer base when it replaced GambetDC as the lottery's subcontractor in April 2024 (OLG testified that the switch brought back more than 22,000 active users from Maryland and Virginia) before converting to a Class A licence under the 2024 Act.

The Class C mobile-only tier is a different business. DraftKings took $26.55m (27.7% share, +2.9% YoY) but its wager count fell 55.1% to 708,912 while average stake rose from $16.34 to $37.45 and hold fell from 8.5% to 6.26%, leaving GGR down 24.5% at $1.66m and tax of $0.50m at the 30% rate. Fanatics took $8.93m (9.3%) at a 6.79% hold for $0.61m GGR, recovering from a negative September (−$48k GGR). bet365, live since 8 Sep 2026 under Hillside LLC, posted $1.59m handle and $183k GGR at an 11.56% hold in its first full month, 1.7% of handle but 2.2% of GGR. Together the three Class C books held 38.7% of October handle but only 29.0% of GGR and paid 38.0% of tax; year-to-date they are 40.8% of handle, 33.7% of GGR and 44.2% of tax. The combination of a 30% rate and sub-7% holds is why PENN withdrew theScore Bet on 23 Feb 2026 after $2.2m of CY2026 handle, and why the tier's economics are the key input to any entry decision.

The other two venue books illustrate the limits of the Class A model when the venue partner is not also the market leader. Caesars at Capital One Arena took $9.82m (+21% YoY) from only 94,890 bets (−75.7%), an average stake of $103.44 and a 4.04% hold, so GGR fell 56% to $396k; its CY2026 hold is 4.25% on $64.7m of handle, which looks like a small number of large, well-informed accounts rather than a mass-market book. BetMGM at Nationals Park took $5.91m at a 9.74% hold for $576k GGR; CY2026 hold 8.03% on $60.2m. Both pay 20% but neither has the retail footfall or brand pull to convert the venue licence into District-wide share. Note also that Caesars' arena landlord, Monumental Sports & Entertainment, has now made bet365 its teams' official betting partner.

On concentration and competitive dynamics: the top two hold 72.6% of handle and 79.2% of GGR; the next three (Caesars, Fanatics, BetMGM) sum to 25.8% of handle and 18.7% of GGR. Per-resident intensity is high — CY2025 handle of $855.6m against roughly 0.7m residents is ~$1,200 per head (our estimate; DC's daytime and visitor population inflates this). Average stake across the market has risen from $26.70 (FY2026) to $32.44 (October), consistent with fewer, larger wagers rather than broader participation. For an operator the message is that share is available from soft-holding incumbents (Caesars, DraftKings) but it must be won on pricing and product, at a 30% tax, against a leader whose 12–13% hold funds promotional reinvestment.

Seasonality and the fiscal calendar matter for planning. OLG's fiscal year runs October to September; FY2026 handle of $881.45m produced $21.97m of tax at a 24.0% blended rate and a 10.38% hold. November 2025 set the GGR record ($11.7m at a 13.16% hold on $89.0m handle); if hold reverts to 10–11% in Nov–Dec 2026, CY2026 GGR lands around $86–88m (estimate), below 2025 even with handle at a record, and tax at ~24% of that is ~$21m versus $22.06m in CY2025.

segments.name: Licensing & tax regime
segments.headline: A three-class, five-year licence system with GGR taxed at 20/10/30% and a $2m ticket for mobile-only entry — expensive by US standards and tied to venues or teams.
narrative: Sports wagering in the District is authorised by the Sports Wagering Lottery Amendment Act of 2018 (DC Code § 36-621.01 et seq.), with operating rules in 30 DCMR Chapter 21 (Privately-Operated Sports Wagering). The Office of Lottery and Gaming, an agency within the Office of the Chief Financial Officer, licenses operators, management services providers, suppliers and occupational licensees, and separately runs the lottery. The original 2019–24 design gave OLG's own GambetDC app (built by Intralot) a District-wide monopoly, with private Class A operators confined to two-block zones around their venues; OLG retained 100% of GambetDC revenue and private licensees paid 10% of GGR. The Sports Wagering Amendment Act of 2024, enacted through the FY2025 Budget Support Act and effective 15 Jul 2024, opened District-wide mobile to Class A licensees, raised their tax to 20%, created the Class C mobile-only licence at 30%, and doubled the Class A application fee from $500k to $1m. OLG's own testimony on the bill (Bill 25-0753) argued the 20%/30% rates were below the ~40% share the District had been retaining from GambetDC and that total revenue would fall unless handle grew; in the event FY2026 tax of $21.97m is up 13% on FY2025 and comfortably above the FY2024 base.

The current fee schedule (DC Code § 36-621.06; OLG Licensing page and Licensing FAQs) is: Class A operator — designated facilities only (Capital One Arena, Audi Field, Nationals Park, St. Elizabeths East Entertainment and Sports Arena), five-year term, $1,000,000 non-refundable application fee, $500,000 renewal, one facility per licence, District-wide mobile rights; Class B operator — retail sportsbooks outside a two-block radius of any Class A facility, $100,000 fee, $50,000 renewal, retail only; Class C operator — created for designated professional sports teams in the District (or their assigned management services provider/operator) to offer District-wide mobile wagering, $2,000,000 fee, renewal reported at $1,000,000. Joint ventures with a Certified Business Enterprise majority partner pay reduced fees ($250k Class A, $25k Class B). OLG may add a processing fee equal to the projected cost of background investigations. Licences are non-transferable. Provisional licences are available to applicants already licensed in an approved jurisdiction, valid six months while the standard application (four to six months) is processed; prerequisites include a DC Basic Business License, an OTR Certificate of Clean Hands, and a surety bond sized to projected tax (OLG guidance illustrates a $1.5m bond on $10m of five-year GGR at 30%). OLG testified that the first three Class C fees generated $6m for the General Fund.

Tax is levied on Gross Sports Wagering Revenue — cash received from wagering less cash paid to players and amounts paid to purchase annuities — at 20% (Class A), 10% (Class B) and 30% (Class C). Operators register with the Office of Tax and Revenue and file monthly return FR-426G by the 20th. Whether promotional credits are deductible is not stated in the OLG materials we read [unverified]; the reported numbers imply they are not materially so, since Class A tax equals exactly 20.0% of reported GGR for every operator. There is no visible loss carry-forward: Fanatics' negative September GGR produced zero tax and its October tax was exactly 30.0% of October GGR. The blended effective rate was 22.9% in October and 24.0% for both CY2026 YTD and FY2026, and it will drift down as FanDuel's Class A share grows and up if Class C books gain share — a feature the CFO's revenue estimates have to live with.

Commercially, DC is one of the most expensive small markets in the US to enter as a mobile-only operator: the $2m Class C fee is comparable to Massachusetts' $5m-per-five-years for a market with roughly a tenth of the population, and the 30% rate is matched only by Pennsylvania (36%), New York (51%), New Hampshire (51%), Rhode Island (51%) and Illinois' top bracket. The 20% Class A rate is competitive, but Class A capacity is physically limited to four designated venues, three of which are taken; the fourth (St. Elizabeths East arena) has no licensee listed and its practical value is unproven. The team-linkage requirement for Class C means entry also carries a sponsorship cost — bet365's MSE deal is the template. Against that, there is no statutory cap on Class B retail licences, the regulator processes provisional licences quickly, and the supplier/MSP route to serve a Class A or B venue is open and cheap relative to operator entry.

segments.name: Retail venues, Class B and the DC Lottery
segments.headline: Retail sports betting is a rounding error (3.6% of FY25 handle) and the lottery's General Fund transfer fell 17% in FY2025 — context for why OLG supports iGaming despite cannibalisation.
narrative: Retail sports wagering in the District exists in three forms: the sportsbooks inside the Class A venues (FanDuel at Audi Field, Caesars at Capital One Arena, BetMGM at Nationals Park), Class B bar/restaurant books, and the legacy OLG-operated retail terminals at lottery retailers that survived the end of GambetDC's mobile app. OLG's FY2025 Progress Report quantifies the split for the first time: retail handle $28.7m (3.6%) against online $773.2m (96.4%), with retail contributing 4% of sports-wagering tax ($773k of $19.39m). The monthly OLG reports do not separate Class A retail from mobile, so there is no October retail figure; the only pure-retail datapoint is the Class B line.

Class B has not worked as a business model. Sports & Social on U Street, the only active Class B licensee, took $21,521 in October (1,176 bets, 7.6% hold, $164 of tax) and $547k year-to-date. The September report still listed Grand Central (Adams Morgan), Cloakbook (K Street), Grand Central H Street and Ugly Mug (Barracks Row) with no activity at all; all four were absent from the October report, which we read as licences lapsed, surrendered or suspended [status unverified against OLG's approved-licence list]. With District-wide mobile available from every major brand, a retail-only licence that cannot offer mobile and must sit two blocks from the arenas has no catchment. For an operator this closes off the cheap ($100k) entry route as anything other than a hospitality amenity.

The DC Lottery is the larger franchise and the political counterweight. FY2025 operating revenue was $210.7m and net revenue $83.4m, but the transfer to the General Fund fell to $32.5m from $39.35m in FY2024 (−17.4%), with the OIG-commissioned audit attributing product-level declines to lower sales across draw games. OLG's traditional-game GGR had turned positive in FY2024 for the first time in several years, so FY2025 is a reversal. Adding $19.3m of private sports-wagering tax, total regulated-gaming transfers reached $51.8m, the highest since FY2017 — meaning sports wagering now supplies roughly 37% of OLG's fiscal contribution, up from zero in FY2019. Lifetime, the lottery has contributed $2.43bn to the General Fund since 1982 and paid $513m in retailer commissions.

OLG also sells e-instant games through DCiLottery, which is the product line most exposed to regulated online casino. Executive Director Burnside told the Council in May 2026 that iGaming would cut into iLottery sales but that casino tax would more than offset the loss; the CFO's fiscal note on B26-0656 puts the lottery hit at $3.4m over FY2027–30 against $47.3m of new gaming tax. The policy stance is therefore that the lottery will absorb cannibalisation in exchange for a higher-yield product it regulates — a reasonable trade for the District, and for a prospective iGaming licensee it removes the usual lottery-lobby obstacle seen in other states.

segments.name: Regulatory direction — iGaming bill B26-0656, sweepstakes and prediction markets
segments.headline: Online casino at an effective 29% of GGR, sweepstakes licensed rather than banned, and a gambling age of 21 are one Council vote series away; prediction markets remain live and untaxed.
narrative: Bill B26-0656, the Internet Gaming and Consumer Protection Act of 2026, was introduced by Ward 7 Councilmember Wendell Felder on 9 Apr 2026, heard by the Committee on Human Services on 4 May (a near four-hour session at which Caesars, DraftKings and BetMGM supported the bill, ARB Interactive/Publishers Clearing House opposed the sweepstakes provisions, and Stop Predatory Gambling opposed the whole measure), and then sat for six months. On 18 Nov 2026 the committee, chaired by Matthew Frumin, reported it out 3-1 with Christina Henderson the lone no. As introduced the bill proposed a 25% tax on adjusted gross internet gaming revenue, a $2m operator application fee with a $500k five-year renewal, a $50k supplier fee ($25k renewal), no cap on operator licences, preference for existing DC sports-wagering licensees, a minimum age of 21 for iGaming, the first $500k of tax to the Department of Behavioral Health, and a ban on dual-currency sweepstakes casinos.

The committee print changed the economics and the perimeter. Tax stays at 25% on adjusted gross internet gaming revenue but live-dealer revenue is taxed at 12.5%, and two further assessments of 2% each — a community-impact assessment and a regulatory assessment — are layered on, taking the effective rate on standard RNG casino to about 29% of adjusted GGR. The renewal fee doubles to $1m per five years. Each licensee may operate no more than two brands, and live-dealer games must be streamed from a studio inside the District staffed by licensed dealers under a labor-peace agreement — a local-content and labour condition that favours operators willing to build a DC studio. Sweepstakes and dual-currency products would no longer be banned outright; anyone offering them would need the same iGaming licence, pay the same tax and follow the same player-protection rules, with OLG and the Attorney General given cease-and-desist and enforcement tools against the unlicensed. Finally, the committee raised the minimum age for all legal gambling other than the lottery to 21, which would move sports betting from 18 to 21. The CFO scores the package at a $246k cost in FY2027 and $62.6m of net new revenue over FY2027–30, including $47.3m of gaming tax, after a $3.4m decline in lottery earnings and $1.8m of lost sports-wagering tax from the age change.

Process risk is now about the calendar, not the committee. The bill needs two readings before the full Council, and the Council period ends in mid-December 2026 (trade reports cite a 15 Dec cut-off for final reading); if it is not passed it lapses and must be reintroduced in 2027. If passed, it goes to the Mayor for signature and then to the 30-day Congressional review that applies to all District legislation, so earliest enactment is Q1 2027, followed by OLG rulemaking and licensing — a realistic launch window of late 2027 to H1 2028 (our estimate). The policy direction is unmistakable even if timing slips: the District has moved in two years from a protectionist lottery monopoly to an open high-tax sportsbook market and now to full online casino with sweepstakes brought inside the tent, while tightening the consumer-protection floor (age 21, mandatory deposit/spend/loss/time limits, 72-hour cooling-off, self-exclusion).

Two unregulated channels frame the enforcement picture. As of 25 Nov 2026 every Kalshi and Polymarket market, including sports event contracts, is available in the District — the CFTC's home jurisdiction — and no District cease-and-desist, lawsuit or OLG guidance against federally registered prediction markets was identified; this contrasts with Washington State, where a court ordered Kalshi to halt sports and election markets in August 2026. Daily fantasy sports likewise operate in DC without a District-specific geofence. Both are untaxed substitutes for a 20–30%-taxed product, and both are a federal-law question the Council cannot resolve. The sweepstakes rewrite is the District's answer on the one channel it can reach: convert the grey market into licence fees and 29% tax rather than litigate it.

segments.name: Payments, responsible gambling & advertising
segments.headline: Card- and ACH-funded, 18+, no credit-card or in-play restrictions and only generic advertising rules — a permissive consumer regime that B26-0656 would tighten on age and limits.
narrative: Payments in the District follow the standard US online pattern — debit card, ACH/online banking, PayPal-type wallets, and operator-branded prepaid cards — with no mobile-money dimension. The District has not banned credit-card funding of wagering accounts (the CASPR scorecard records the ban as not in place), nor does it impose a deposit-to-bet waiting period. Operators must verify identity and physical location; secondary guidance indicates new customers may deposit and wager for up to 30 days before completing verification, but must verify before their first withdrawal. Geolocation is to the District boundary, which matters commercially because a large share of DC's weekday population lives in Maryland and Virginia, both of which have their own licensed mobile markets — the OLG testified that moving the lottery's app to FanDuel in 2024 repatriated more than 22,000 active users who had been betting across the border.

The statutory minimum age for sports wagering and lottery is 18, lower than the 21 that applies in most US states; BetMGM and Caesars apply 21 by house policy. The committee print of B26-0656 would raise the age for all non-lottery gambling to 21, which the CFO estimates would cost $1.8m of sports-wagering tax over four years — implying the 18–20 cohort is roughly 2% of GGR (our inference from the CFO figure). In-play betting and micro-markets are permitted; there are no statutory stake, deposit or loss limits for sports betting today, although operators offer deposit, wager and time limits as account tools (FanDuel's DC house rules describe these), and the iGaming bill would make deposit, spend, loss and time limits plus a 72-hour cooling-off mandatory.

Responsible-gambling obligations sit in 30 DCMR §§ 2128–2129: each operator must have an OLG-approved responsible-gaming plan, display problem-gambling and self-exclusion information with the 1-800-522-4700 helpline on signage, websites and apps, and state the consequences of underage play. OLG runs a single District-wide Self-Exclusion Program covering lottery products, DCiLottery, Class A/B retail sportsbooks (since 1 Mar 2022) and all mobile apps; a single application excludes the person from every licensed channel, bars them from receiving gambling advertising, promotional offers or complimentary goods, and terms run from 18 months to lifetime (secondary source; OLG's page does not list durations). Problem-gambling services are publicly funded through the Department of Behavioral Health, and the iGaming bill would route the first tranche of casino tax there.

Advertising is permitted and lightly constrained (30 DCMR § 2131): advertisements must carry problem-gambling and self-exclusion information and the helpline, be socially responsible, present a balanced message about winning and losing, and state that the operator is licensed by OLG; Class B operators may not place physical advertising within two blocks of a Class A venue; and no gambling marketing may be sent to self-excluded persons. There are no time-of-day, venue, college-campus or stadium-signage restrictions and no tobacco-style warnings, which is why the CASPR state scorecard gives the District an 'F'. For an entrant this is a low-friction marketing environment — team partnerships with in-broadcast odds integration (bet365/Monumental Game Center) are explicitly allowed — but the direction of travel under B26-0656 is toward tighter limits, and an operator should underwrite on the assumption that the age floor rises to 21 and mandatory limit tools arrive within the licence term.

highlights.text: Volume is at a record and still edging up: October handle of $95.76m is the highest month since the 2020 launch, FY2026 handle grew 9.9% to $881.45m and CY2026 YTD is +3.8%; a ~$1,200-per-resident handle intensity (estimate) reflects a dense, affluent, commuter-swollen population that over-indexes on mobile betting.

Hold is cyclically depressed, so GGR has mechanical upside: CY2026 hold of 9.69% compares with 11.1% in CY2025 and 10.4% in FY2026; a reversion to 10.5–11% on the same handle adds $6–9m of annual market GGR without any volume growth (estimate).

iGaming is closer than in any other US jurisdiction without a land-based casino: B26-0656 passed committee 3-1 on 18 Nov 2026 with a 25% headline rate (12.5% live dealer), two brands per licence, no licence cap and the lottery regulator openly supporting it; a $50k supplier licence is a cheap B2B entry point if it passes.

New entrants can ramp quickly despite incumbency: bet365 went from launch (8 Sep 2026) to $1.59m monthly handle at an 11.56% hold in its first full month on a team partnership (Capitals, Wizards, Mystics) with in-broadcast odds integration — a template the advertising rules permit.

Share is available from soft-holding incumbents: DraftKings (6.26% hold, bet count −55% YoY), Caesars (4.04%, average stake $103) and Fanatics (5.48% CY hold) are ceding GGR share to FanDuel; a better-priced, parlay-led product could take share without needing the market to grow.

The regulator has a track record of outsourcing: OLG replaced its Intralot-built GambetDC app with FanDuel as subcontractor in 2024 before converting it to a licence, and still runs retail wagering and DCiLottery — a platform/managed-services supplier to OLG or a Class A/B/C licensee faces a $10k–$50k licence rather than a $2m one.

Tax and licensing rules are stable: no pending change to the 20/10/30% sports-wagering rates or fees was identified, and the FY2026 tax outturn ($21.97m, +13%) gives the CFO no revenue reason to reopen them.

lowlights.text: Class C unit economics are thin: a 30% GGR tax plus a $2m five-year fee, a mandatory team tie-up and the market's 6.6% Class C hold mean a 5% handle share (~$57m/yr) yields only ~$3.9m after tax before marketing (estimate) — PENN exited after 13 months and $2.2m of CY2026 handle.

The market is small and now ex-growth on handle: +0.9% YoY in October, a ~$90m GGR pool, and two operators holding 79% of GGR; FanDuel's venue licence (20% tax, 12.8% CY hold) gives it a structural cost advantage of roughly 10 points of GGR over any Class C challenger.

Tax take is falling even as handle rises: October tax −1.7% YoY and CY2026E tax of ~$21m versus $22.06m in 2025 (estimate), because mix is shifting to 20%-taxed Class A books and hold is down; a CFO looking for revenue could revisit the Class A rate or promo deductibility.

Age 21 and mandatory limits are in the committee print of B26-0656: sports betting would lose the 18–20 cohort (CFO: −$1.8m tax over FY2027–30) and all operators would need deposit/spend/loss/time-limit tooling and a 72-hour cooling-off — modest in revenue terms but a compliance build.

Prediction markets are an untaxed, unlicensed substitute operating openly in the CFTC's home city: all Kalshi and Polymarket sports markets are live in DC with no District enforcement, and DFS runs without a geofence; both erode the addressable pool for a 30%-taxed licensee.

The sweepstakes rewrite legalises a competitor class: by licensing dual-currency operators under iGaming rather than banning them, the committee print could let incumbent social-casino brands with existing DC databases convert into licensed rivals on day one.

Retail and Class B do not work: retail is 3.6% of handle, the sole active Class B book took $21.5k in October, and four Class B venues went dormant and were delisted; the lottery's own transfer fell 17.4% in FY2025, so OLG's fiscal pressure (and appetite for cannibalising products) is rising.

forecast.intro: There is no issuer guidance for a market; the bridge below moves from the CY2025 actuals to our CY2026 estimate using OLG's January–October actuals plus Nov–Dec at last year's seasonality (+2–4%, with bet365 incremental) and a 10–11% hold. The result is a record on handle (~$886–889m) but a decline on GGR (~$86–88m) and tax (~$21m) because hold has compressed from 11.1% to ~9.7–10%. The swing factors over the next 12–24 months are regulatory rather than volumetric: whether B26-0656 clears two full-Council readings before the mid-December close of the Council period, whether the age-21 and sweepstakes-licensing provisions survive, and whether the District ever moves against prediction markets.

forecast.view: **Sports betting:** we expect FY2027 (Oct-26 to Sep-27) handle of ~$900–930m (+2–6%) with bet365 adding 2–4 points of share from DraftKings, Fanatics and Caesars rather than from FanDuel, and GGR of ~$90–97m as hold mean-reverts toward 10–10.5%; tax ~$21.5–23m (all estimates). If age 21 is enacted mid-2027, trim handle by ~1–2%. **Concentration rises:** FanDuel's Class A cost advantage and 12–13% hold should take it above 60% of GGR; we expect one further Class C exit or merger-driven withdrawal within two years unless iGaming cross-sell arrives. **Online casino:** our base case (55%) is that B26-0656 passes the full Council in December 2026, clears Congressional review in Q1 2027, and launches in late 2027–H1 2028 at an effective ~29% rate on RNG casino and 16.5% on live dealer; iGaming GGR in year one of ~$60–90m (estimate, benchmarked to per-capita yields in Michigan and New Jersey discounted for DC's two-brand cap and in-District studio requirement) would roughly double OLG-regulated private gaming tax. **Leverage/fiscal direction:** the District's dependence on private gaming tax rises from ~37% of OLG transfers today toward half; that makes future rate increases less likely, not more, provided volumes hold. **Enforcement:** expect OLG and the AG to use the new sweepstakes powers quickly once enacted, but no action against CFTC-registered prediction markets absent a federal ruling.

Per-resident handle, CY2026E/FY2027E and iGaming year-one figures are our estimates and labelled as such. FX: the market reports in USD; no currency conversion applied.
